name: pyannote.audio
purpose: Neural speaker-diarisation toolkit providing pretrained pipelines for voice activity detection, speaker segmentation, embedding and clustering, answering 'who spoke when' in an audio recording.
journalism_use_case: The de facto open diarisation layer for newsroom pipelines: separating speakers in interviews, conference calls and intercepted audio before transcription, so a transcript attributes each statement to a person rather than producing an undifferentiated wall of text.
pros: The reference open diarisation implementation — WhisperX, noScribe and most newsroom transcription stacks depend on it, so it is the de facto standard
Very actively developed with a 4.x line (4.1.0 released 2026-11-17) and an exceptionally clean tracker (35 open issues against 10,806 stars)
MIT licensed with the project stating the pipeline 'will always remain open-source' on its model card — a meaningful commitment given the commercial arm
Modular: VAD, segmentation and embedding components can be used separately or retrained on your own audio
cons: Weights are gated: the speaker-diarization-3.1 model card requires agreeing to share your HuggingFace information to access the model — a real blocker for air-gapped work and a disclosure for anonymity-sensitive users, since the model authors learn your identity at download time
Accuracy drops materially on overlapping speech, telephone-band audio and recordings with many speakers — exactly the conditions of covertly recorded material
Increasingly coupled to a commercial offering (pyannote.ai) whose Precision models are better than the open ones, creating a structural incentive toward the paid tier
Engineer-facing: no UI, and tuning clustering parameters for a specific recording type takes experimentation
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented and checkable: the HuggingFace model card for pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1 states the information-sharing requirement and also states the pipeline will remain open source. The commercial pyannote.ai price list was verified in session 1: Diarization Precision-3 batch at EUR0.112/hour of audio, Community-1 batch EUR0.035/hour, Live-1 streaming EUR0.198/hour, plus Developer EUR19/month and Starter EUR99/month subscriptions (vendor page, 2026-11-16).
assessment: Necessary rather than optional if you need speaker attribution, and the gating is a manageable but real nuisance: download the weights once on a non-sensitive machine with an organisational HuggingFace account, then distribute internally so individual journalists never authenticate. For media-in-exile work that one-time disclosure matters and should be a deliberate decision. Where diarisation accuracy on bad audio is critical, benchmark against NeMo Sortformer — but note Sortformer's CC-BY-NC licence blocks commercial publication.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 4.1.0 published the same day, 10,806 stars, 35 open issues. Same-day push and release plus a very low backlog at scale; the commercial arm appears to sustain rather than starve the open project, though that balance is worth monitoring.
model_or_data_licence: MIT but GATED — the speaker-diarization-3.1 card requires agreeing to share your HuggingFace information to access the model. The card also states the pipeline will remain open-source.
licence_restrictions: No field-of-use restriction, but access is conditioned on identity disclosure to HuggingFace and the model authors. That is an access barrier with privacy consequences rather than a licence limitation.
costs: Open library free. GPU recommended for throughput. The hosted pyannote.ai alternative is priced per audio-hour (Precision-3 batch EUR0.112/h; Community-1 batch EUR0.035/h; Live-1 EUR0.198/h) with Developer EUR19/month and Starter EUR99/month tiers including matching credit — verified 2026-11-16, EUR, usage-based. Using the hosted service means uploading audio.
privacy: Inference is local and audio stays on your machine. The gate is the privacy cost: obtaining weights discloses your HuggingFace identity. Pre-staging weights solves this for downstream users. Never use the hosted API for source-sensitive audio.
alternatives: NVIDIA NeMo Sortformer for higher accuracy — but CC-BY-NC-4.0 blocks commercial publication
WhisperX, which wraps pyannote with alignment and transcription
Accepting unlabelled transcripts where speaker attribution is not editorially necessary
blockers: Gated weights requiring HuggingFace identity disclosure — plan a one-time central download for air-gapped or anonymity-sensitive deployments

name: PyMuPDF
purpose: Python bindings to MuPDF providing fast text and image extraction, page rendering, annotation, document assembly and true redaction that removes underlying content.
journalism_use_case: Fastest route to rasterising pages for OCR at corpus scale, and — critically — to applying genuine redactions that delete the underlying text rather than drawing a black rectangle over it. That distinction is a documented real-world newsroom failure mode: published PDFs whose 'redactions' were copy-pasteable.
pros: True redaction (apply_redactions removes the content stream text) prevents the single most embarrassing and dangerous document-publishing failure in journalism
Significantly faster than pdfminer-based libraries for rendering and bulk text extraction, which matters when rasterising hundreds of thousands of pages
Very actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-17, release 2.1 on 2026-11-02) with a small backlog (79 open issues against 11,147 stars)
Single bundled dependency (MuPDF) makes deployment simple compared with Ghostscript-dependent alternatives
cons: AGPL-3.0 is the decisive caveat: embedding PyMuPDF in a network-facing newsroom service triggers source-release obligations unless you buy Artifex's commercial licence — and the commercial price is not publicly listed
The dual-licence model means your compliance position depends on how you deploy, not just what you build — an easy thing to get wrong late in a project
API has changed across major versions (1.x to 2.x naming), so older tutorials and code break
Rendering fidelity and text-extraction ordering can differ from pdfplumber, so results are not interchangeable between libraries
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: AGPL-3.0 confirmed via GitHub API and the repository licence; Artifex's commercial licensing is advertised on its site without a public price (quote required, not verified here). 11,147 stars, 79 open issues, release 2026-11-02.
assessment: Use it for internal batch processing and redaction, where AGPL is harmless; think carefully before putting it inside a public-facing service. For your profile the redaction capability alone justifies having it in the toolkit — I would build a small internal redaction utility around it rather than relying on a GUI tool. If you need a permissive alternative for a product you ship, pypdf (BSD-style) or pdfminer.six cover extraction but not fast rendering or true redaction.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 2.1 (2026-11-02), 11,147 stars, 79 open issues. Commercial vendor backing with frequent releases and prompt issue handling.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (dual-licensed; Artifex sells a commercial licence)
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft is material: offering a modified or even unmodified PyMuPDF-based service over a network obliges you to provide corresponding source under AGPL terms, unless you hold Artifex's commercial licence. Commercial licence price is not publicly listed — quote required.
costs: Free under AGPL-3.0. Commercial licence from Artifex: price not publicly listed (quote required, not verified in this survey). No infrastructure beyond Python; CPU-bound.
privacy: Fully local, no network calls. Good fit for isolated evidence machines.
alternatives: pypdf (BSD-3-Clause) for licence-clean extraction and page manipulation
pdfplumber for auditable coordinate-level extraction
Ghostscript/qpdf for rasterisation if AGPL is unacceptable and you can tolerate slower performance
blockers: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft if deployed inside a public-facing service without a commercial licence

name: RapidFuzz
purpose: Fast C++-backed string-similarity library implementing Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler, token-set and partial-ratio scorers with batch cdist operations over large candidate lists.
journalism_use_case: The low-level primitive under most name matching: score a leaked client list against a sanctions or PEP list, or cluster near-identical company names, without fuzzywuzzy's GPL licensing and with orders-of-magnitude better speed on million-pair comparisons.
pros: MIT licence resolves a real problem — fuzzywuzzy, the tool most tutorials teach, is GPL-licensed and awkward inside a commercial newsroom codebase
Fast enough to brute-force comparisons that would otherwise need blocking, which simplifies small-to-medium matching jobs considerably
Multiple scorers with clear semantics, so you can choose a metric suited to the name form (token_set for reordered names, partial for substrings)
Actively maintained, light dependency footprint (optional numpy), trivially auditable
cons: A metric library, not a matching system: no blocking, no clustering, no threshold guidance, so you must build the matching logic and defend the thresholds yourself

Raw edit distance mismatches transliterated and reordered names — Mohammed/Muhammad, surname-first registries, patronymics — which is precisely where investigative name matching lives, so normalisation (rigour) is required first
No probabilistic interpretation: a score of 87 means nothing editorially, unlike Splink's match weight
GitHub release metadata is slightly inconsistent (latest release tagged v3.14.6-1 versus tag v3.14.6), a minor pinning annoyance
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 4,208 stars, 43 open issues, active commits (pushed 2026-11-09). RapidFuzz is a widely used drop-in replacement for fuzzywuzzy, which is verifiable from its own documentation and from downstream adoption.
assessment: Keep it installed; it is the right primitive and the MIT licence makes it the correct default over fuzzywuzzy. But understand its place in the stack: normalise with rigour, block sensibly, score with RapidFuzz, then adjudicate with a human or escalate to Splink for a defensible probability. Treating a RapidFuzz score as a match decision is the most common way newsroom name-matching goes wrong.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, latest release v3.14.6-1 (2026-08-30), 4,208 stars, 43 open issues. Steady releases on a 3.x line with current commits from an engaged single maintainer.
licence_restrictions: None — and specifically it avoids fuzzywuzzy's GPL constraint.
costs: No fee, negligible resources. CPU only.
privacy: Entirely local, no network, no models.
alternatives: rigour for the normalisation step that must precede it
Splink where you need auditable match probabilities
datasketch for document-level rather than string-level similarity

name: rigour
purpose: Library of data-cleaning primitives for investigative data: name normalisation and fingerprinting, company-type canonicalisation, address parsing, country and language code handling, and identifier validation (IBAN, LEI, ISIN, tax numbers).
journalism_use_case: The unglamorous preprocessing that decides whether matching works at all: turning 'OOO Rosneft-Trading Ltd.' and 'ROSNEFT TRADING LIMITED' into the same key before any fuzzy scorer sees them, and validating that a claimed IBAN or company number in a leak is structurally real.
pros: Encodes domain knowledge that is tedious and error-prone to reimplement: legal-form suffixes across dozens of jurisdictions, company-type equivalences, identifier checksums
Supersedes the widely cited 'fingerprints' package — using rigour instead is itself a useful piece of knowledge, since fingerprints is the one most tutorials reference
Identifier validation catches fabricated or mistyped IBANs/LEIs in a dataset, a cheap integrity check that catches real data problems
Actively released (v2.6.2, 2026-11-07) under MIT by the organisation that runs the largest open sanctions dataset
cons: Normalisation rules are tuned for Latin-script corporate and sanctions data and are weaker on CJK and Arabic name forms, so non-Western corpora need additional handling
Small community (73 stars, 16 open issues) — effectively an OpenSanctions internal library published openly, so documentation assumes their context
Normalisation is lossy: the fingerprint is a matching key, not a display value, and conflating the two corrupts published names
Bundled reference datasets (country codes, legal forms) go stale and are updated on the maintainer's cadence, not yours
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Production evidence is structural and checkable: rigour is a dependency of nomenklatura and the OpenSanctions pipeline, which processes a continuously updated multi-source entity dataset.
assessment: Adopt it as the first stage of any name-matching work — the quality gain from correct normalisation exceeds what a better fuzzy scorer gives you, and it is the cheapest improvement available. For your profile the specific action is to replace any use of the older fingerprints package with rigour. For CJK and Arabic material, supplement with uroman or script-specific handling rather than trusting the defaults.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-07, latest release v2.6.2 published the same day, 73 stars, 16 open issues. Frequent releases driven by production needs at OpenSanctions; small but current.
model_or_data_licence: Bundled reference datasets (country codes, legal forms) — permissive, derived from public standards.
alternatives: nomenklatura for the resolution stage that follows normalisation
RapidFuzz for the scoring stage
uroman for romanising non-Latin scripts before normalisation

name: sentence-transformers
purpose: Framework for computing dense sentence and passage embeddings with hundreds of pretrained models, supporting semantic search, clustering, cross-encoder reranking and fine-tuning.
journalism_use_case: Query a multilingual leak in your own language and retrieve semantically matching passages in others — searching Russian correspondence with an English query. Also used to align a translation against its original and to find near-duplicate documents across language editions of the same press release.
pros: Cross-lingual retrieval with LaBSE or multilingual-e5 solves a problem keyword search fundamentally cannot, and is the single most useful AI capability for cross-border reporting
Permissive weights verified for the common choices: Apache-2.0 for sentence-transformers/LaBSE and MIT for intfloat/multilingual-e5-large, both read from their HuggingFace cards
Now maintained under the huggingface organisation (transfer verified this session), with a v6.3.0 release on 2026-11-11 — stronger institutional footing than the original academic home
Fine-tuning on your own domain is documented and practical, which matters for jargon-heavy corpora
cons: Embedding quality degrades substantially for low-resource languages, so the cross-lingual promise is uneven precisely where exile-media reporting often works
Returns passages, not translations — an MT or human step is still required, and a retrieved passage can be misread without it
You must build the index, storage and UI yourself; 1,321 open issues reflect the breadth of integration questions this creates

Semantic search has no recall guarantee: a document that does not surface is indistinguishable from one that does not exist, which is dangerous in investigative work where absence is sometimes the finding
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: repository transfer from UKPLab to huggingface, confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17; 19,289 stars with 1,321 open issues — wide adoption with a very large backlog. Model licences read from HuggingFace cards in session 1 and retained.
assessment: Adopt, with an explicit methodological rule: semantic search supplements keyword search, never replaces it, because you cannot evidence what it failed to retrieve. For your profile the combination to standardise on is multilingual-e5-large (MIT) for retrieval plus a keyword index for completeness, with both results shown to reporters. Pre-stage the weights for air-gapped operation.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v6.3.0 (2026-11-11), 19,289 stars, 1,321 open issues. Recent major release under new Hugging Face stewardship; the enormous backlog is a support-capacity signal, not a decline signal.
model_or_data_licence: Apache-2.0 for sentence-transformers/LaBSE; MIT for intfloat/multilingual-e5-large (both read from their HuggingFace cards). Other checkpoints vary and must be checked individually.
licence_restrictions: Code and the two verified checkpoints are unrestricted. The hazard is checkpoint-specific: some popular embedding models carry non-commercial terms.
costs: No fee. GPU strongly recommended for embedding large corpora (hours versus days); inference for queries is cheap on CPU. Vector storage adds a FAISS index or vector DB. Infrastructure estimate.
privacy: Local after model download; no text leaves the machine. Pre-stage weights for air-gapped work. The risk to avoid is configuring a hosted embedding API, which would transmit every document.
alternatives: txtai to get embeddings plus index plus search in one dependency
BERTopic for clustering rather than retrieval
Apache Solr or OpenSearch with their own vector support if you already run them

name: sherpa-onnx
purpose: ONNX-Runtime-based speech toolkit providing streaming and offline ASR, TTS, VAD, speaker identification and keyword spotting with bindings for a dozen languages and builds for Android, iOS, Raspberry Pi and desktop.
journalism_use_case: Transcription on locked-down or offline hardware — field laptops, phones, a Raspberry Pi in a monitoring setup — for hostile-environment reporting where sending audio to any server, or even installing Python and PyTorch, is unacceptable.
pros: Explicitly built for no-internet operation on constrained devices, which is the specific requirement that disqualifies most of the transcription stack here
Extremely broad platform and language-binding support (Android, iOS, embedded, C/C++/Rust/Go/Swift/Kotlin), so it embeds into a custom field application
Streaming ASR enables live monitoring use cases — a radio or broadcast feed transcribed continuously on local hardware
Very active (pushed 2026-11-17) with frequent prebuilt artefact releases, so you rarely compile from source
cons: Model-zoo quality varies widely by language, and the best models are English and Chinese; a minority-language deployment may be unusable
Diarisation and speaker handling are simpler than pyannote or NeMo Sortformer
Sprawling documentation with many model/runtime combinations, and you must match versions carefully — 648 open issues reflects this complexity
Release tagging is chaotic (latest release artefacts carry names like 'react-fa'), making version pinning awkward
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 16,005 stars with 648 open issues and continuous commits. The Next-gen Kaldi project has an established research reputation; no journalism deployment verified.
assessment: The correct choice for a narrow but important case: embedded or field transcription with no network. For routine newsroom transcription, whisper.cpp is simpler and has better multilingual quality. For your profile I would reach for sherpa-onnx when building something — a monitoring appliance, a phone app for reporters in the field — rather than when transcribing files. Evaluate the specific language model before committing, since quality variance is the main risk.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, frequent release artefacts, 16,005 stars, 648 open issues. High commit velocity with institutional research backing; release hygiene is poor but activity is unambiguous.
model_or_data_licence: Varies per exported checkpoint (Whisper, Zipformer, Paraformer and others distributed separately) — verify the specific model.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Checkpoint licences vary; some research models carry non-commercial terms, so check the specific archive you deploy.
costs: No fee. Runs on existing or cheap hardware (a Raspberry Pi class device suffices for small models), which is part of the point. Engineering time for integration is the real cost.
privacy: Designed for no-internet operation; nothing leaves the device. Among the strongest privacy profiles in the catalogue, and the right building block for a field device that must not phone home.
alternatives: whisper.cpp for simpler CPU transcription of files
faster-whisper for server-side batch throughput
Vosk as an older alternative for embedded offline ASR

name: spaCy
purpose: Production-oriented NLP library providing tokenisation, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, named-entity recognition and rule-based matching, with trained pipelines for around 25 languages.
journalism_use_case: Baseline workhorse for pulling person, organisation, location and money mentions out of leaked documents and mailboxes. The EntityRuler is the feature that matters most in practice: reporters supply a gazetteer of target names and companies, and the pipeline flags every occurrence across a corpus before any statistical NER runs.
pros: Fast, stable and predictable at corpus scale — the practical default when you need to process a million documents on CPU without GPU infrastructure
EntityRuler and the Matcher let you encode editorial knowledge (target lists, aliases) deterministically, which is both more accurate and more defensible than a statistical guess
Documentation is the best in the NLP ecosystem and the API has been stable for years, so pipelines keep working
MIT licensed with mostly-MIT English pipelines, and a commercially sustainable company behind it
cons: Statistical NER degrades noticeably on OCR-noisy leak text, unusual transliterations and non-Latin scripts — exactly the material investigations contain
No entity linking to real-world identifiers out of the box, so 'Rosneft' stays a string rather than becoming an entity
Fixed label set unless you retrain, which makes investigation-specific types (vessel, shell company) impractical — GLiNER is the better answer there
Model package licences vary: en_core_web_* are MIT but some non-English packages carry corpus-derived terms, and these were not individually verified
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 34,061 stars, 276 open issues, pushed 2026-10-27 with release-v3.8.18 (2026-10-26) and a v4.0.0.dev10 tag in progress. spaCy is a dependency of Presidio and many newsroom pipelines, which is verifiable from those projects.
assessment: Adopt as the baseline, but use it the right way round: gazetteer matching first (high precision, defensible), statistical NER second (recall, needs review). For your profile the honest limitation is non-Latin scripts and OCR noise, where Stanza or GLiNER will outperform it — keep all three available and choose per corpus rather than standardising on one.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-27, latest release release-v3.8.18 (2026-10-26), tag v4.0.0.dev10, 34,061 stars, 276 open issues. Regular 3.8.x maintenance releases plus a v4 development line; commercial company backing. Three weeks since last push is normal for a mature library.
model_or_data_licence: Varies by pipeline package: en_core_web_* are MIT; some non-English packages carry corpus-derived terms. Not individually verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. Check the specific language pipeline's licence before commercial use — a few derive from restrictively licensed treebanks.
costs: No fee. CPU-efficient; large-scale NER over millions of documents is a compute-hours cost on commodity hardware. Explosion sells Prodigy (annotation tool) separately — a paid product, price not verified here, and not required.
privacy: Local-only inference; only the initial model download touches the network. Suitable for air-gapped work once packages are staged.
alternatives: GLiNER for investigation-specific custom entity types
Stanza for better non-English accuracy
entity-fishing when you need Wikidata identifiers rather than strings

name: Splink
maintainer: UK Ministry of Justice Analytical Services
purpose: Probabilistic record-linkage library implementing the Fellegi-Sunter model with unsupervised parameter estimation (expectation maximisation), running on DuckDB, Spark, Athena or Postgres backends, with diagnostic visualisations.
journalism_use_case: Link people across two large datasets with no shared key — a sanctions list against a corporate registry, or a leak's client list against a property register — at a scale where dedupe would stall, and with auditable per-comparison match weights you can show an editor or a lawyer.
pros: Produces an interpretable match weight per comparison rather than an opaque score, which is the difference between a defensible linkage and an assertion — the single most important property for published investigations
Scales to tens of millions of records on a laptop via the DuckDB backend, which removes the infrastructure barrier that normally forces this work into a cluster
Built and used by a government analytical service for operational data linkage, with published methodology — strong institutional provenance
Excellent diagnostic charts (match weight waterfalls, parameter estimates) that make the model's behaviour inspectable rather than magical
cons: Requires genuine understanding of blocking rules and m/u probabilities; naive use produces confidently wrong links, and the library will not stop you
Output is a probability, not a verdict — the adjudication threshold is an editorial decision that must be documented, and teams often skip that step
v5 broke APIs relative to v3/v4, while most tutorials and blog posts still circulating describe the older versions — a real friction point (221 open issues)
No built-in UI for human adjudication of borderline pairs, so you must build that review step yourself
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: MoJ Analytical Services is the maintainer and publishes its methodology, which is credible institutional production evidence; 2,588 stars, 221 open issues, v5.0.0 released 2026-09-18. Note that the v5 API break against widely circulating v3/v4 tutorials is verifiable from the project's own migration documentation.
assessment: My recommended record-linkage tool for your work, replacing dedupe. The reason is specifically evidentiary: when a story asserts that two records are the same person, Splink lets you state the match weight and the comparison features that produced it. Budget time to learn the model properly — this is the one tool here where shallow use is actively dangerous — and build a small review interface for pairs above your threshold.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-11, latest release v5.0.0 (2026-09-18), 2,588 stars, 221 open issues. A major release in 2026 with current commits and public-sector institutional backing.
costs: No fee. DuckDB backend runs locally with no infrastructure. Spark/Athena backends incur cloud costs and would move data to that infrastructure — avoid for sensitive linkage. Estimate.
privacy: Local with the DuckDB backend, which is the recommended configuration for sensitive data. Choosing a cloud Spark or Athena backend relocates the data to that provider — a configuration decision with major privacy consequences.
alternatives: nomenklatura if your data is already in FollowTheMoney
dedupe for small analyst-driven jobs, with its maintenance caveat
RapidFuzz plus manual rules for trivially small matching tasks

name: Stanza
purpose: Neural NLP pipeline covering tokenisation, lemmatisation, POS tagging, dependency parsing, NER and coreference for 70+ languages, with a Python bridge to Java CoreNLP.
journalism_use_case: Entity extraction from non-English leaks — Russian, Arabic, Ukrainian and Chinese registries and correspondence — where English-first pipelines fail. It is also the bridge to CoreNLP's SUTime for normalising the date expressions that structure a timeline from narrative documents.
pros: Language coverage (70+) is the broadest in this subcategory and the specific reason to carry it alongside spaCy for cross-border work
CoreNLP bridge gives access to SUTime date normalisation and OpenIE relation extraction, neither of which spaCy provides
Academically grounded with consistent Universal Dependencies annotations, so cross-language processing is methodologically coherent
Actively released (v1.15.1, 2026-11-14) with a long institutional track record at Stanford
cons: Model licensing is the open question: the code is Apache-2.0 (verified by reading the LICENSE file, since GitHub reports 'Other'), but the Available Models documentation page states no licence for the downloadable model archives, and training treebanks and NER corpora may carry their own restrictions — an unresolved commercial-use risk
Slower than spaCy by a wide margin on large corpora because the models are heavier neural pipelines
NER label sets vary by language, so merging entities across languages needs a mapping layer you build yourself
103 open issues and an academic support model — responses are not guaranteed
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The documented finding carried forward and retained here is the licensing gap: GitHub SPDX reports NOASSERTION, the LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 (Copyright 2019 Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University), and the models page states no licence for the model archives. That combination is a genuine unresolved risk, not an oversight in this survey.
assessment: Carry it specifically for non-English material, where it is the strongest open option. But treat the model licensing as an open compliance question before anything built on it is commercially published: the code licence is clear and the weights licence is not. For your profile I would ask Stanford directly or restrict Stanza's output to internal lead generation rather than published derived datasets until that is resolved. Marking this entry's licence confidence as medium for exactly that reason.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-15, latest release v1.15.1 (2026-11-14), 7,917 stars, 103 open issues. Current releases on a 1.15.x line with university backing; sustained over many years.
licence: Apache-2.0 (GitHub licence detection reports 'Other'; the LICENSE file read directly is the Apache License 2.0, Copyright 2019 Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University)
model_or_data_licence: NOT verified and materially uncertain — the Available Models documentation page states no licence for the downloadable model archives, and training treebanks/NER corpora may carry their own restrictions.
licence_restrictions: Code is permissive. Model archives have no stated licence, so commercial redistribution of outputs or weights is legally unclear. Treat as an open question, not a permission.
costs: No fee. GPU recommended for large corpora; CPU is workable but slow. CoreNLP bridge adds a JVM. Estimate.
privacy: Local inference; model archives downloaded from Stanford or HuggingFace on first use. No inference-time network calls.
alternatives: spaCy for speed on major languages
GLiNER for custom entity types with a clearer Apache-2.0 weights path
PaddleOCR/PP-Structure plus GLiNER for CJK document pipelines
blockers: Model-archive licence is unstated — unresolved commercial-use risk for derived published datasets

name: Subtitle Edit
purpose: Desktop subtitle editor supporting 200+ subtitle formats with waveform and spectrogram display, synchronisation tools, OCR of hardcoded subtitles, and integrated Whisper transcription backends.
journalism_use_case: Turning raw transcripts into broadcast-ready captions, and precisely re-timing or verifying subtitles on leaked or downloaded video evidence against the waveform — including OCR-ing burned-in subtitles from a video where no transcript exists, which is a common verification task on circulated clips.
pros: Waveform and spectrogram view makes manual verification of what was actually said at a given moment practical for a non-engineer — the cheapest route to audio verification
Subtitle OCR extracts text from burned-in captions, a capability almost nothing else in this catalogue offers and which matters for verifying re-uploaded or re-captioned clips
Integrated Whisper backends mean transcription and caption editing happen in one tool
Extremely active (pushed 2026-11-17, release v5.4.0 2026-11-06) and mature after many years
cons: Windows-centric: the native build is Windows and other platforms rely on Wine or a less complete port, which is a real constraint in a mixed newsroom
Online machine-translation features call third-party services and would send subtitle text off-machine — must be switched off by policy for sensitive material
Dense UI aimed at professional subtitlers rather than reporters; the learning curve is non-trivial despite the GUI
199 open issues; feature breadth means edge-case bugs across the 200+ formats
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 15,028 stars with 199 open issues, same-day push on 2026-11-17 and a release on 2026-11-06 — sustained single-maintainer activity over more than a decade. Widely used in the subtitling community; no journalism deployment verified.
assessment: Useful in two distinct roles: caption production for published video, and forensic verification of what a clip actually says. For your profile the second is the more interesting one — the spectrogram plus subtitle-OCR combination is a genuine verification capability. The controls needed are a Windows machine (or a tested Wine setup) and switching off the online translation services before any sensitive file is opened.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v5.4.0 (2026-11-06), tag v5.5.0-beta8, 15,028 stars, 199 open issues. Continuous development with regular releases and betas from a long-standing maintainer.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the editor; bundled Whisper backends use MIT weights.
costs: Free. No infrastructure. Optional Whisper backends run locally. If online MT is enabled, third-party service terms and possible costs apply — not priced here.
privacy: Local by default. The explicit exception is the optional machine-translation features, which transmit subtitle text to third-party services; disable them for any sensitive file. Subtitle OCR and waveform analysis are entirely local.
